newsitem.title: UK: Jobs to go as UK's BBC restructures production.
newsitem.headline: Jobs to go as UK's BBC restructures production.

text.p: The BBC said on Wednesday that jobs would be lost as it set up a new structure uniting its radio and television programme making departments for the first time .
The BBC Production unit combines the 4,000 staff who make the majority of the corporation's non-news programmes.
"When the new structure is fully up and running there will be less than 4,000 people but I can't be specific about the numbers," said BBC Production chief executive Ronald Neil.
Some potential job cuts may be offset by programme opportunities in digital channels. The aim is to cut costs by 30 million stg next year and 70 million annually by 2001/2002.
The new structure was prompted by reforms introduced by BBC Director-General John Birt last June when he announced plans to separate commissioning and scheduling from production.
At the same time Birt introduced a new management structure which critics said favoured television over national radio and the world service.

The BBC said the new production structure would enable it to develop "centres of excellence" in areas such as Science, Music, Arts and Sport. BBC Production comprises 18 units compared to 36 under the old set-up.
It will make 600 million stg of radio and television programmes each year for existing channels and develop additional output for planned digital and online services.
English langugage staff from the World Service will be integrated into the operation from next April.

"Bringing the World Service's English language service into the Production family will have to be managed imaginatively, with a real understanding of listeners' needs," said BBC Director of Programmes Alan Yentob.
Director-General Birt last month had to modify his plans to integrate World Service news into the main body of BBC current affairs following pressure from politicians and listeners.
Under a compromise agreement, World Service news and current affairs programmes will be produced by a dedicated unit within BBC News.
